before.text: On June 28, 1914, Archduke Franz Ferdinand rode through the streets of Sarajevo in an open car.
A young Bosnian Serb in the crowd shot and killed him.
Thirty-seven days later, Europe's great powers were at war.
So how did one assassination drag a whole continent into war?
Picture a schoolyard where every kid has promised to back up a friend in any fight.
When two kids start shoving, their friends pile in, then their friends' friends.
In 1914, the two kids were Austria-Hungary and Serbia, and the promises were the alliance system.
Here is the story's line-up, in the order each joins it.
The alliance system had split Europe into two camps.
Germany was allied with Austria-Hungary, while Russia was allied with France and backed Serbia.
Britain stood loosely with France and Russia, without a firm promise to fight.
But promises alone don't start wars, and Europe was already tense.
First, militarism: the powers raced to build bigger armies and navies.
Then nationalism: Serbian nationalists wanted Bosnia's Serbs united with Serbia.
But Austria-Hungary had annexed Bosnia in 1908, so it saw Serbia as a threat to its empire.
Back on the timeline, Franz Ferdinand was heir to Austria-Hungary's throne.
Because his killer, Gavrilo Princip, was a Bosnian Serb, Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia.
Germany promised Austria-Hungary its full support.
On July 28, Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia: that's the first shove.
A common mistake is to think the assassination alone caused the war.
It was only the spark; the long-term tensions turned a local fight into a European war.
What do you think Russia did next?
Russia mobilized its army to protect Serbia.
Germany saw that as a threat, so it declared war on Russia on August 1.
Two days later, it declared war on Russia's ally, France.
Germany's Schlieffen Plan was to defeat France quickly, so it could avoid fighting on two fronts at once.
The quickest road to France ran through neutral Belgium, so on August 4, German troops marched in.
Britain had promised in 1839 to protect Belgium's neutrality.
So that same day, Britain declared war on Germany.
Now, how did a European war become a world war?
Japan had been allied with Britain since 1902.
So on August 23, 1914, Japan declared war on Germany, and the fighting spread to Asia.
Alliances chained Europe's tense powers together, so one assassination pulled them into war one by one.
That's how one shooting in Sarajevo became a world war, one promise at a time.
